# Data Sources

We use three data sources from three different organizations: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Museum of Modern Art, and the Conflict Catalog (Peter Brecke, Georgia Tech).

## Source A: The Met Open Access

(maybe add image here somewhere)

**Issues reading this source:** 'Object Date' is free text (ex: "19th century"), so we drop it and use the numeric 'Object Begin Date / 'Object End Date' columns instead. Many columns are empty so we need to find a way to address that (drop or fill?).

## Source B: MoMA Collection

(maybe add image here somewhere)

**Issues reading this source:** 'ArtistBio', 'Nationality', and 'Gender' are wrapped in parentheses, and 'Date' mixes formats ("1896", "1976-77", "c. 1917").

## Source C: Conflict Catalog

(maybe add image here somewhere)

# Course set up

```{r}
# Checks that R and each package are installed and new enough for this course.
# Stops with a list of everything that needs fixing, and how to fix it.
check_course_versions <- function(required, area) {
  problems <- character(0)
  to_install <- character(0)
  found <- character(0)
  for (name in names(required)) {
    need <- required[[name]]
    if (name == "R") {
      have <- getRversion()
      if (have < need) {
        problems <- c(problems, sprintf(
          "R is version %s; this course needs %s or newer. Install the current R from https://cran.r-project.org/ (see https://howisonlab.github.io/datawrangling/current/rtidyverse/rstudio_installation.html), then reinstall your packages.",
          have, need))
      }
      found <- c(found, paste("R", have))
    } else if (!nzchar(system.file(package = name))) {
      problems <- c(problems, sprintf("%s is not installed.", name))
      to_install <- c(to_install, name)
    } else {
      have <- packageVersion(name)
      if (have < need) {
        problems <- c(problems, sprintf(
          "%s is version %s; this course needs %s or newer.", name, have, need))
        to_install <- c(to_install, name)
      } else if (isNamespaceLoaded(name) && getNamespaceVersion(name) != have) {
        problems <- c(problems, sprintf(
          "%s %s is installed, but this R session is still using %s. Restart R.",
          name, have, getNamespaceVersion(name)))
      }
      found <- c(found, paste(name, have))
    }
  }
  if (length(problems) > 0) {
    fix <- "In RStudio choose Session > Restart R"
    if (length(to_install) > 0) {
      fix <- paste0(fix, ", then run this in the Console:\n  install.packages(c(",
                    paste0('"', to_install, '"', collapse = ", "), "))\n")
    }
    stop("Course setup (", area, ") found problems:\n  - ",
         paste(problems, collapse = "\n  - "), "\n\n",
         fix, "\nThen run the setup chunk(s) again.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  cat("Course setup OK (", area, "): ", paste(found, collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "")
}

check_course_versions(c(
  R = "4.5.0",         # CRAN builds Mac/Windows packages for the current and previous R only
  tidyverse = "2.0.0",
  dplyr = "1.2.0",     # recode_values() and replace_values()

  gt = "1.0.0",        # needed by gtExtras
  gtExtras = "0.6.1"   # works with ggplot2 4
), "R")

library(tidyverse)

library(gtExtras)
```

```{r}
head(met_raw)
```

### Load Source B: MoMA

```{r}
head(moma_raw)
```

## Cleaning

### **Cleaning the Met dataset:**

- Keep only Object Name = painting (for now)

- Keep only paintings from 1400 - 2000 (this is the only range the Conflict Catalog covers)

- Pick which columns to keep: Object Name, Title, Artist Display Name, Artist Nationality, Artist Gender, Object Begin Date, Object End Date, Medium, Tags, Tags Wikidata URL

Keep the paintings from 1400 to 1999, the years the Conflict Catalog covers.

```{r}

met_clean <- met_raw |>
  filter(`Object Name` == "Painting") |>                              
  filter(`Object Begin Date` >= 1400 & `Object Begin Date` < 2000)     # 5936 rows

met_clean
```

Keep the columns of interest

```{r}
met_clean <- met_clean |>
  select(object_name = 'Object Name',
         title = Title,
         artist = 'Artist Display Name',
         nationality = 'Artist Nationality',
         gender = 'Artist Gender',
         start_year = 'Object Begin Date',
         end_year = 'Object End Date',
         medium = Medium,
         tags = Tags,
         tags_wikidata_url = 'Tags Wikidata URL')

met_clean
```

Paintings by several artists list them with \|, e.g. “William P. Babcock\|Jules Guerin\|Louis Philibert Debucourt”, and their nationalities & genders are also listed similarly. Splitting them into multiple rows:

```{r}
met_clean <- met_clean |>
  mutate(painting_id = row_number()) |>
  separate_longer_delim(c(artist, nationality, gender), delim = "|")

met_clean
```

Checking if split happened successfully:

```{r}
check <- met_clean |>
  filter(artist %in% c("Jules Guerin", "Louis Philibert Debucourt"))

check

```

### **Cleaning the MoMA dataset:**

- Keep only Classification = painting (for now)

- Keep only paintings before 2000

- Pick which columns to keep: Classification, Title, Artist, Nationality, Gender, Date, Medium

Columns in the Met dataset which don't have corresponding columns in the MoMA (we need to find how to populate these):

- The Met has Object begin & end dates, the MoMA has just "date". This can be repeated in 2 columns start year & end year (they can be the same if there is only 1 date, or they can be different if the date is a range - this will have to be done using CaseWhen, probably).

- The Met has tags but the MoMA doesn't. There may be tags about paintings online?? Or can we use AI to do this??

Keep only paintings

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_raw |>
  filter(Classification == "Painting")   # 2458 rows

moma_clean
```

Keep only the columns of interest

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  select(
    object_name = 'Classification', 
    title = 'Title', 
    artist = 'Artist', 
    nationality = 'Nationality', 
    gender = 'Gender', 
    date = 'Date', 
    medium = 'Medium')

moma_clean
```

Break up the date into pieces so we can build a start and end year to match the Met. We first tried doing this directly with `case_when`, but it kept throwing errors, so we split out every possible piece first and assemble them afterwards.

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  separate_wider_regex(
    date,
    patterns = c(
      before = ".*?",                # text before the year, like "c. "
      start_century = "\\d{2}",      # "19" in 1930
      start_years = "\\d{2}",        # "30" in 1930
      dash = "\\s*[-–]?\\s*",        # dash between years
      end_years = "\\d*",            # "33" in 1930-33, or "1935" in 1930-1935
      after = ".*"                   # leftover text, like "s" in "1910s"
    ),
    too_few = "align_start"          # don't error on rows with no or incomplete dates
  )

moma_clean
```

Build the start year from the century and year pieces: "19" and "30" become 1930.

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  mutate(start_year = as.numeric(start_century) * 100 + as.numeric(start_years))

moma_clean
```

Build the end year: - a 4-digit end ("1930-1935") is used as it is - a 2-digit end ("1930-33") takes the start's century, so 1933 - no end year means the end is the same as the start

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  mutate(end_year = case_when(
    str_length(end_years) == 4 ~ as.numeric(end_years),
    str_length(end_years) == 2 ~ as.numeric(start_century) * 100 + as.numeric(end_years),
    TRUE ~ start_year
  ))

moma_clean
```

If the end year is in the next century ("1898-02"), the step above gives 1802, which is before the start, so we add 100 to get 1902.

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  mutate(end_year = case_when(
    end_year < start_year ~ end_year + 100,
    TRUE ~ end_year
  ))

moma_clean
```

Remove paintings with no date, and paintings from 2000 onwards (outside the Conflict Catalog's years).

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  drop_na(start_year) |>
  filter(start_year < 2000)   # 2225 rows

moma_clean
```

Drop the temporary columns we made while splitting the date.

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  select(object_name, title, artist, nationality, gender, medium, start_year, end_year)

moma_clean
```

Remove the brackets from Nationality: “(American)” becomes “American”. For group works like “(American) (French)” we keep the first.

```{r}
moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  separate_wider_regex(nationality,
                       patterns = c("\\(", nationality = ".*?", "\\).*"))

moma_clean
```

Do the same for Gender: “(male)” becomes “male”.

```{r}

moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  separate_wider_regex(gender,
                       patterns = c("\\(", gender = ".*?", "\\).*"))

moma_clean
```

An empty “()” leaves "", which we turn into missing.

```{r}

moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  mutate(nationality = na_if(nationality, ""),
         gender = na_if(gender, ""))

moma_clean
```

### **Cleaning the Conflict Catalog:**

- Keep only rows with more than 1000 fatalities

- Columns to keep: Name, Start Year, End Year, TotalFatalities, Region, Decade

Keep conflicts with 1,000+ deaths, then drop any without both years.

```{r}
conflict_clean <- conflict_raw |>
  filter(TotalFatalities >= 1000) |>     # 1033 rows
  drop_na(StartYear, EndYear)            # 1024 rows

conflict_clean
```

Keep the columns of interest

```{r}

conflict_clean <- conflict_clean |>
  select(common_name = 'Common Name',
         name = 'Name',
         start_year = 'StartYear',
         end_year = 'EndYear',
         total_fatalities = 'TotalFatalities',
         region = 'Region',
         decade = 'Decade')

conflict_clean
```

Split the years off the end of the name: “France-Siam, 1892-93” becomes “France-Siam” and “1892-93”.

```{r}

conflict_clean <- conflict_clean |>
  separate_wider_regex(name,
                       patterns = c(conflict = ".*",
                                    ",\\s*",
                                    name_years = "\\d{4}.*"),
                       too_few = "align_start",
                       cols_remove = FALSE)

conflict_clean
```

First we tried to split the notes on who is fighting into "country" and "actors" by splitting on the dash:

*Split contents of "Name" column into 2:*

- *Country: first comma-separated part goes into Country*

- *Actors (i.e. people who are fighting): second comma-separated part goes into Actors*

But here are multiple participating countries in many conflicts (more than two), so simply splitting on the dash will not work. There are also many extra info like "China (minority in Hebei, Shandong, Anhui, Jiangsu)".

So we decided to organise the table such that:

- Every conflict - participant pair has one row

- Original name is still retained for context

```{r}
conflict_split <- conflict_clean |>
  mutate(conflict_id = row_number(),   # so rows from the same conflict stay linked
         participant = conflict) |>    # split a copy; keep the original text for context
  
  # 1. Split on dashes: "Muscovy-Poland, Lithuania" -> "Muscovy" / "Poland, Lithuania"
  separate_longer_delim(participant, delim = "-") |>
  
  # 2. Remove notes and stray parentheses: "China (Ming)" -> "China", "(Poland" -> "Poland"
  separate_wider_regex(participant,
                       patterns = c(
                         open        = "\\(?",     # an optional "(" at the start
                         participant = "[^()]*",   # everything up to the next parenthesis
                         note        = ".*"        # the rest: "(Ming)", ")" etc.
                       )) |>
  
  # 3. Split comma lists: "Poland, Lithuania" -> "Poland" / "Lithuania"
  separate_longer_delim(participant, delim = ",") |>
  mutate(participant = str_trim(participant)) |>
  filter(participant != "") |>
  select(-open)

conflict_split
```

Region mapped from *Brecke (1999), "Violent Conflicts 1400 A.D. to the Present in Different Regions of the World"*. The paper doesn't define -9; but it is used once, for World War II, so we labelled it ourselves (probably refers to multiple regions?).

the link: https://peregrinosxlapaz.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Brecke-PSS-1999-paper-Violent-Conflicts-1400-AD-to-the-Present.pdf

```{r}
region_lookup <- tribble(
  ~region, ~region_name,
  1,  "North America, Central America, and the Caribbean",
  2,  "South America",
  3,  "Europe west of 15°E, plus Sweden and Italy",
  4,  "Europe east of 15°E, including the Caucasus",
  5,  "Middle East",
  6,  "North Africa",
  7,  "West & Central Africa",
  8,  "East & South Africa",
  9,  "Central Asia",
  10, "South Asia",
  11, "Southeast Asia",
  12, "East Asia",
  -9, "Multiple regions (our label)"
)

conflict_clean <- conflict_clean |>
  left_join(region_lookup, by = join_by(region))

conflict_clean
```

## Transformations

The Met & MoMA datasets now have the same schema (table below).

| Common column    | Met source          | MoMA source          |
|------------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| `museum`         | “Met” (added by us) | “MoMA” (added by us) |
| `title`          | Title               | Title                |
| `artist`         | Artist Display Name | Artist               |
| `nationality`    | Artist Nationality  | Nationality          |
| `gender`         | Artist Gender       | Gender               |
| `start_year`     | Object Begin Date   | Start Year           |
| `end_year`       | Object End Date     | End Year             |
| `medium`         | Medium              | Medium               |
| `tags`           | Tags                | Tags                 |
| `classification` | Object Name         | Classification       |

- Adding a new column to the Met table "museum", and the values for this will be "Met" for all.

```{r}
# adding a new museum column with values "met" to the met table (to identify met paintings when we merge later)

met_clean <- met_clean |>
  mutate(museum = "Met")

met_clean
```

```{r}
# adding a similar column with values "moma" to the moma dataset 

moma_clean <- moma_clean |>
  mutate(museum = "moma") |>
  mutate(tags = "placeholder", tags_wikidata_url = "will drop later")

moma_clean
```

- Appending the rows from the MoMA table to the Met dataset.

```{r}
museums_combined <- rows_append(met_clean, moma_clean)

museums_combined
```

### Joining the countries lookup table to conflicts table

We need a way to compare the artists' nationalities in the museums table to the countries in the conflict catalog. So, we need a lookup table that matches a standard, modern country name with a "raw value" that covers:

- nationalities (demonyms)

- common country names used in the conflict catalog

- and old country names used in the museum datasets & conflict catalog (eg - Holy Roman Empire, Soviet Union, etc)

```{r}
nationality_lookup <- read_csv("nationality_lookup.csv")
```

We want to assign a "standard country" name to all the historical countries used in the conflict catalog. We will use this standard country name to compare with paintings from the museum dataset.

```{r}
lag_years <- 10   # window for how long after a conflict we want to compare paintings with conflicts 

conflict_std <- conflict_split |>
  left_join(nationality_lookup |> select(raw_value, standard_country),
            by = join_by(participant == raw_value)) |>
  mutate(after_end = end_year + lag_years) |> # after_end gives us the extra range after the conflict ends in which we want to see the paintings
  select(conflict_id, conflict, participant, note, standard_country, conflict_start = start_year, conflict_end = end_year, after_end, fatalities = total_fatalities) |> # renaming columns so they don't clash with the museum table columns
  drop_na(standard_country) #dropping ones with no match so that NA doesn't get matched with NA when joining with museum table 

conflict_std
```

### Joining the countries lookup table to the museums table 

We started to left join the nationalities lookup table, then realised that some were giving no matches because there is extra information written after the nationality for some rows (eg: "American, born Germany").

Both present nationality & birthplace may be relevant for our analysis, but for now we are sticking to present nationality and dropping the birthplace, since the birthplace is also not consistently entered across all the artists' info. Many artists who are born elsewhere have not been logged as such. We might come back to this if we have time at the end.

Removing the extras at the end of nationality:

```{r}
museums_combined <- museums_combined |>
  # Clean the nationality to match on
  separate_wider_regex(nationality,
                       patterns = c(
                         nat_main = "[^(),]*", # everything up to the comma 
                         extra = ".*"        # the rest like ", born Germany", etc
                       ),
                       cols_remove = FALSE) |>  # keep the original nationality column
  mutate(nat_main = str_trim(nat_main))

museums_combined
```

Looking up the standard country and joining:

```{r}
museums_std <- museums_combined |>
  left_join(nationality_lookup |> select(raw_value, standard_country),
          by = join_by(nat_main == raw_value))

museums_std
```

Just noticed that painting id is not unique across the rows (because we stacked met & moma IDs), so adding a new column with a unique ID:

```{r}
museums_std <- museums_std |>
  mutate(painting_id = str_glue("{museum}-{painting_id}"))

museums_std
```

### Joining the conflict catalog to the museum datasets 

After this join, each row in the table will be one painting-conflict match.

```{r}
painting_conflicts <- museums_std |>
  left_join(conflict_std,
            by = join_by(standard_country,
                         start_year >= conflict_start,
                         start_year <= after_end),
            relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(timing = case_when(
    is.na(conflict_id)         ~ "none",     # no matching conflict
    start_year <= conflict_end ~ "during",
    TRUE                       ~ "after"
  ))

painting_conflicts
```

## **Is a painting morbid or not?**

- We will create a lookup table "morbidity" of morbid keywords (tags) from the Met & MoMA datasets. Each keyword will have a classification of "is_morbid" or "not_morbid".

- We will left join the "morbidity" to the combined Met & MoMA dataset on the keywords column. If a keyword from the "morbidity" table's keyword column is present in the combined table's keyword list, the corresponding classification is added to the left table. (I'm actually not sure if this is how it works?? Or if the values in the cells need to be exactly equal for a join)

We need to create a lookup table for country names, and then compare with the country names being used in each of the datasets.

We will add a "standardised country name" column to the three datasets by joining the lookup table.

Then we will join the Conflicts table (left join) to the Met & MoMA combined table on the "standardised country name" column.

Assign a "crisis_status":

- during: painted between start_year and end_year of a conflict in the artist’s country

- after: painted 1–10 years after a conflict ended

- none: no matching conflict

- Assumption is that we treat the artist’s nationality as where the painting was made. This won’t always be true but it is a compromise for now.

## Analysis

We will do some aggregations to determine whether paintings are more morbid when conflicts happen:

- Group by crisis_status (during / after / none) and calculate the share of morbid paintings in each group. Present it as a table and bar chart.

- Group by decade and plot the share of morbid paintings next to the total conflict fatalities per decade. Can also check the correlation for the same decade and with a one-decade lag (fatalities in decade *t* vs. morbidity in decade *t+1*)

- For countries with enough paintings (e.g. 100+), compare the morbid share in conflict years with non-conflict years in the same country. We can see if some countries/cultures produce more morbid art by default.

- Check whether large conflicts are linked to a bigger increase than small ones (still thinking through how to do this one)
